newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: Swiss damage from U.S. Nazi gold report seen limited.
newsitem.headline: Swiss damage from U.S. Nazi gold report seen limited.

text.p: Switzerland may be able to limit any political damage from a major U.S. report on Nazi gold by citing the host of concessions it has made to calm international criticism of its World War Two role, analysts said on Wednesday.
But it may face renewed demands for Holocaust compensation from world Jewish groups as a result of the U.S. government report, unveiled in Washington earlier in the day.

The U.S. study on the amount and fate of Nazi German gold stolen from occupied countries and Holocaust victims criticised Switzerland's "business as usual" post-war attitude in resisting the return of looted Nazi gold as "inexplicable".

"It is hard to say exactly what the reaction abroad will be. But it seems that few new facts will emerge and that the outrage over Switzerland will thus not be as great as it was earlier," said Hans Hirter at the Institute for Swiss Political Science in the capital, Berne.
He and other analysts spoke before the report was published.
Berne was braced to react swiftly once the report was unveiled, though officials denied they had been given an advance look by the Clinton administration.
Berne's troubleshooter for Holocaust issues, special ambassador Thomas Borer, was in Washington to make a statement if required.

Hirter said the Swiss government and banks had already soothed critics, led by the World Jewish Congress (WJC), with a long list of efforts to uncover and atone for the wartime past, including creating a Holocaust memorial fund with 265 million Swiss francs ($181.2 million) in donations from banks and businesses.

Other steps included lifting bank secrecy for two independent panels, one hunting for unclaimed bank accounts left by Holocaust victims and another writing a broad history of the Swiss wartime role as a financial centre.

Switzerland has also proposed selling some official gold reserves to finance a seven billion Swiss franc humanitarian foundation, although officials say this has nothing to do with making amends for its wartime and post-war attitude.
"These things show Switzerland is willing to deal with its past and therefore the critics are likely willing to say that Switzerland is doing something already to atone," Hirter said.

But the U.S. report, compiled by 11 agencies led by Undersecretary of Commerce Stuart Eizenstat, could spur new demands for compensation from world Jewish groups, according to Gian Trepp, author of an authoritative 1993 study of Nazi gold movements through the Bank for International Settlements (BIS).

"If the U.S. report puts a number on the gold that Switzerland bought and the number is much higher than has been acknowledged so far, then this could lead to new demands," the Swiss historian told Reuters.
"This possibility cannot be ruled out," he said.
Switzerland paid the Allies 250 million Swiss francs in gold under a 1946 accord settling claims against the neutral state for buying stolen Nazi gold.
Switzerland's central bank has acknowledged buying 1.2 billion Swiss francs of Nazi gold at 1940s prices, much of which it now says must have been stolen from occupied countries.

But the Bank says it never had any evidence the gold from Hitler's Reichsbank was smelted from the stolen possessions of concentration camp victims, such as jewelry and gold teeth. ($ = 1.462 Swiss Francs)
